title: Beautifying a mitzvah
hookLine: lovely candlesticks, a fine cup, a hand-made challah cover
tomorrow: the custom nobody remembers starting. what's yours?

cards: People spend an hour choosing the right font for a birthday card that gets read once. The Kiddush blessing works the same over a paper cup as over a silver one.
So why does the tradition bother with a beautiful cup at all? One question for today: does beauty matter to God?

teach.h: THIS IS MY GOD, I WILL GLORIFY HIM.
teach.b: The rabbis start from one line of the song at the sea: "This is my God, and I will glorify Him." The Talmud, in Shabbat, reads glorify as adorn: make yourself beautiful before God in mitzvot.

teach.h: ADORN THE MITZVAH: CUP, SCROLL, SUKKAH.
teach.b: A beautiful sukkah, a beautiful shofar, a Torah scroll written in fine ink with a fine pen by a skilled scribe. The name is hiddur mitzvah, beautifying a commandment.
The Talmud even sets a measure: for hiddur mitzvah, spend up to a third more. So the tradition's answer is yes, with a limit. Beauty doesn't make the blessing work.
It says the blessing matters. Polished candlesticks on Friday afternoon. A hand-made challah cover.
And a neighbor says something close.

teach.h: GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.
teach.b: In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says God is beautiful and loves beauty. Jews and Muslims both hold that beauty and God belong together. One honest difference.
In the hadith, the line answers a man worried that liking fine clothes and shoes is pride: beauty in how a person presents themselves isn't arrogance.
In the Talmud, the beauty goes into the objects of a commandment: the cup, the scroll, the sukkah. Both make room for beauty. They place it in different spots.

how: Jews beautify mitzvot with fine Kiddush cups, candlesticks, embroidered challah covers, decorated sukkot and handsome Torah scroll covers, and the Talmud allows spending up to a third more for the sake of beauty.

o: buying the costliest ritual items you can
a blessing said over new clothes or shoes

games.q: beauty and the mitzvah — tap the pairs.
p: God is beautiful and loves beauty

s: a mitzvah done with a plain object doesn't count
beauty adds honor; the mitzvah stands either way.
the Talmud sets a measure: up to a third more for beauty
Jews and Muslims place beauty in exactly the same things
both link beauty and God; the hadith speaks of a person's dress, the Talmud of mitzvah objects.

games.q: a friend buys a plain plastic menorah to save money, then feels she's done it wrong. what does hiddur mitzvah suggest?
o: it's still the mitzvah; beauty is extra, up to a third more if she can.
it doesn't count unless the menorah is beautiful.
she should buy the most expensive one she can find.
games.why: beauty honors the mitzvah, within a measure. the lighting itself is the mitzvah.

practice: Pick up one object you use for something that matters to you: a cup, a candleholder, a pen, a bowl. Wipe it slowly with a cloth or your sleeve until it shines a little. Then set it down somewhere it can be seen.

wordCard.voice: Hiddur mitzvah: beautifying a commandment, from this is my God, and I will glorify Him. The cup matters because of what's said over it.

orig.note: Hebrew: the beautifying of a commandment.

carryVoice: Pocket it: beautiful mitzvot, a cup or a candlestick polished on a Friday afternoon. Fourteen of fifteen, shining.

sources.q: This is my God, and I will glorify Him
